How It's Made Hydrogen Fuel Cells
So... is it prohibitively expensive to manufacture these things, or is there another reason we don't see more of them in cars/trucks/etc?

Hydrogen fuel cells have really only been the target of serious research for commercial applications for a short time. It is hard to economically produce the hydrogen, store it for long periods of time, compress it, and also store it safely for use on vehicles. Hydrogen gas is flammable, and contribute to the oxidation of certain metals. Additionally it must be pressurized to fit within a small volume. Many current fuel cell designs use platinum as part of the catalyst in the PEMs. Platinum is very expensive, and even those there's just a small bit of it, the cost for all the membranes adds up.

The use of hydrogen fuel cells in vehicles is also fairly rare, because there aren't many places that will sell the hydrogen fuel currently (the fact that hydrogen fuel cells are rare also makes it hard for gas stations to justify getting equipment to sell the fuel to so few customers, so the problem is somewhat cyclical.) Because these fuel cells are rarely used, not many of them get manufactured, so they don't benefit much from an economy of scale. Many of these fuel cells are prototypes or proofs-of-concept, and there's an extra cost associated with manufacturing a complex, non-standard machine.

Politically, hydrogen fuel cells are unfortunately a bit of an ugly duckling. Their competition for convenience and versatility are fossil fuels, but those are cheaper by many margins due to fossil fuel's highly developed supply chain, subsidies, and a large economy of scale. Their competition for non-CO2 emitting energy storage are lithium and lithium ion batteries, but those have been the focus of commercial research for many years, are used in other devices such as computers, and quite frankly that industry has done a far better job lobbying and marketing itself as the clean-energy alternative and thus is also subsidized.

The engineering problems associated with making hydrogen fuel cells feasible are not insolvable; Experiments are showing that Graphene or a carbon-nanotube mixture can be used to supplement or substitute the platinum used in the PEMs. It is possible to generate H2 gas very quickly by combining water and aluminum (which generates hydrogen gas and aluminum oxide) which could negate the need for long term hydrogen storage. However, developing these technologies would take time and money, and there aren't many large agencies or companies that are investing as much of either into hydrogen fuel cell tech as they are with fossil fuels or lithium batteries. Even if fuel cell tech became more commercially viable, it is hard to get a new technology like this adopted by the population at large. People would not buy fuel cell vehicles unless they knew they could refuel them easily, and companies would not invest in creating refueling services unless there was a supply of vehicles to buy their fuel. Fossil fuels have a large established infrastructure supporting them, while conventional batteries can tap directly into the electricity infrastructure across most countries and to the manufacturing infrastructure that makes devices such as laptop and cellphone batteries.

Lastly, most steps along the chain of hydrogen production and storage require electricity. In order for hydrogen to be truly a zero-carbon fuel, that electricity must come from clean energy sources.

The mass adoption of hydrogen fuel cells could very well be technologically possible with some research but is unlikely due to economic reasons and competition from more established technologies. However we may see adoption and use in the future on vehicles like trains, large trucks and boats.

One place that hydrogen fuel cells do have a very bright future is in space exploration, as most modern spacecraft designs already include a supply of liquid hydrogen and have need of a low-weight, reliable electric generator.
